# Query understanding

Google rewrites pretty much every query before looking it up: it detects the language (falling back on location and browser settings for brand-only queries), drops stop words, recognises entities and expands the query with synonyms, so a short query can become a much longer internal one. Its synonyms are learned from search behaviour rather than catalogued by linguists, so words people use interchangeably count as synonyms, while 'siblings' such as Canon and Nikon are kept apart, and spellings with and without diacritics are generally treated as the same. Google's How Search Works page confirms the synonym and spelling systems; stop words, siblings and the rewriting detail were said at the event and are not in Google's docs. Fan-out queries from the AI features pass through the same query understanding, which also predicts which result types a query gets, using historical interaction data for ambiguous queries such as 'orange'. Query processing deliberately mirrors indexing, as Day 2 said of word segmentation, and the diacritics point extends Day 2's statement that Google usually understands words with or without accents; Google's summary slide added that typos and plurals need no attention because Google rewrites them automatically. Day 1's second recording put this at the start of serving: Cherry Prommawin said serving begins by interpreting the query, cleaning it up, detecting its language and expanding it; Gary Illyes contrasted 1990s searchers who had to 'speak machine' with today's natural-language queries, and said MUM helps interpret the context of query words. On Day 2 the non-Latin-script talk added that users may type the same Persian query in their own script or in Latin letters with the same intent, as Google's 2023 post on multilingual searches describes for Hindi.

Based on: `D3-C006`, `D3-C008`, `D3-C012`, `D3-C016`, `D3-C018`, `D3-C028`, `D3-C029`, `D3-C036`, `D3-C038`, `D3-C039`, `D3-C040`, `D3-C048`, `D3-C087`, `D3-C059`, `D3-C062`, `D3-C304`, `D3-C309`, `D3-C310`, `D3-C013`, `D2-C321`, `D2-C600`, `D3-C067`, `D1-C215`, `D1-C186`, `D1-C218`, `D2-C965`, `D2-C981`.

## What to do

- Write each page in the words its audience uses; do not add synonym lists or every spelling variant, which Google expands itself.
- Search for each variant of a key term before writing: if the variants bring up the same entity, pick one; if a phrase returns unrelated results, use that phrase where it matters.
- On multilingual sites, annotate language versions with hreflang, because a brand-only query does not tell Google which language the user wants.

  <br><sub>`D3-C304` · Day 3, How Search results are born (Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Extends [D3-C004](../../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** When the query itself names the wanted result type, as 'pictures' does in 'orange pictures' (or a query asking for videos or news), Google can read the intent directly from that word.
  <br><sub>`D3-C305` · Day 3, How Search results are born (Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Visual Elements gallery of Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/visual-elements-gallery), [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For an ambiguous query such as 'orange', Google uses historical data: it looks at how users reacted to different kinds of results for previous and similar queries and shows the result types users prefer.
  <br><sub>`D3-C309` · Day 3, How Search results are born (Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google handles an image used as a search query much like a text query interpreted as an embedding: the image is broken down into vectors (embeddings) that are then searched for in the index.
  <br><sub>`D3-C311` · Day 3, How Search results are born (Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C740](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Repeats [D1-C224](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google can still detect intent for image queries, even though they are searched as embeddings, the speaker said.
  <br><sub>`D3-C312` · Day 3, How Search results are born (Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Behind the visible attributes, small pieces of product data such as brand and UPC or other barcodes are very important for Google Shopping's query understanding, retrieval and ranking.
  <br><sub>`D3-C356` · Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links (Alex Jansen) · consistent with Google docs · [Product data specification](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7052112?hl=en)</sub>

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's post on multilingual searches (8 September 2023) says that, because of typing difficulty on some keyboards, a person in India might search in Hindi using Latin rather than Devanagari characters and want and receive Hindi results written either way.
  <br><sub>`D2-C981` · Search Central blog (8 September 2023) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [How Google Search handles multilingual searches](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/09/multilingual-searches) · Used by `DEV-INT-11`, the glossary term *Transliterated queries*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's How Search Works page says understanding a query ranges from recognising and correcting spelling mistakes to a synonym system that finds relevant documents without the exact words searched, such as 'adjust laptop brightness' for 'change laptop brightness'.
  <br><sub>`D3-C087` · Google Search (How Search Works) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's How Search Works page says the language models it builds to match a query's few words to the most useful content took over five years to develop and significantly improve results in over 30% of searches across languages.
  <br><sub>`D3-C088` · Google Search (How Search Works) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's SEO Starter Guide advises anticipating the different words readers search with (some search for 'charcuterie', others for 'cheese board') but not worrying about every variation, because Google's language matching systems relate pages to queries without the exact terms.
  <br><sub>`D3-C089` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Help says the language of search results is chosen from the language of the query, the user's Google language setting, the device's languages and the user's location, which helps when a word such as 'taxi' is the same in several languages.
  <br><sub>`D3-C090` · Google Search Help · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [How Google knows what language to show in search results](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/13511324?hl=en)</sub>

- **[Docs]** A 2006 Search Central blog post says Google considers pages with and without accents for a query word (México and Mexico), and that which accented characters count as equivalent depends on the searcher's interface language.
  <br><sub>`D3-C091` · Search Central blog (1 September 2006) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [How search results may differ based on accented characters and interface languages](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2006/08/how-search-results-may-differ-based-on)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's How Search Works pages say Google uses aggregated and anonymized interaction data to assess whether search results are relevant to queries, turning that data into signals for its machine-learned systems.
  <br><sub>`D3-C310` · Google Search (How Search Works) · annotates Day 3, How Search results are born · is the documentation · [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/)</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Write each page in the words its audience uses and drop synonym lists added for search engines: Google adds synonyms at query time, and blocks of keyword variants read as keyword stuffing, which Google's spam policies prohibit.
  <br><sub>`D3-C024` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · Used by `DEV-INT-11`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Before writing, search for each variant of a key term: if the variants bring up the same entity or near-identical results, use the term your audience uses; if one variant returns unrelated results, write that variant on the page.
  <br><sub>`D3-C047` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For audiences that type the same words in two scripts or spellings (Hindi in Devanagari and in Latin letters, German with and without umlauts), check which forms appear in Search Console's queries and use those forms in headings and key text.
  <br><sub>`D3-C055` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · Used by `DEV-INT-11`</sub>
